claims.text: The proposed alloy system is CoCrFeMnNi-based with a minor Pd addition of approximately 2–5 at.%.
Slower cooling promotes the formation of short-range-order clusters in Pd-modified CoCrFeMnNi alloys.
Short-range-order clusters act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The dislocation barriers produced by short-range order increase hardness relative to rapid quenching.
The dislocation barriers produced by short-range order increase yield strength relative to rapid quenching.
Homogenization at 1100°C for 2 hours ensures chemical uniformity.
The controlled comparison uses water quenching as the baseline and furnace cooling at 1°C/min to 600°C followed by quenching as the intervention.
Diffuse-scattering features in X-ray diffraction can characterize the extent of short-range order in these specimens.
High-resolution TEM imaging can provide atomic-scale evidence of short-range-order clusters in these specimens.
An optimal cooling rate can produce strengthening short-range order without causing phase separation.
Slow-cooled specimens will exhibit more short-range order than rapidly water-quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled specimens will have higher hardness than rapidly water-quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled specimens will have higher yield strength than rapidly water-quenched specimens.
Excessively slow cooling may cause phase separation or secondary-phase formation.
Phase separation caused by excessively slow cooling may degrade the strengthening effect.
Rapidly water-quenched specimens have minimal short-range-order development.
The hypothesis is limited to cooling conditions that promote short-range order without inducing phase separation or other secondary phases.
Local-composition variations and other strengthening mechanisms may affect the quantitative contribution attributed to short-range order.
Failure of slow cooling to produce a statistically significant increase in short-range order would falsify the proposed cooling-to-ordering relationship.
An increase in short-range order without corresponding increases in hardness and yield strength would falsify the proposed strengthening mechanism.
